note: RoleMiddleware index => [super, support]. Both roles may LIST users; only super may change them (below).
RoleMiddleware store => [super]. Creating a user is the classic privilege-escalation route: a support account that reaches this can mint itself a super.
RoleMiddleware update => [super]. Includes the role column, so a support account reaching this can promote itself.
RoleMiddleware store => [super]. Writes server connection settings.

CronScriptController store => [super]. These scripts run over SSH on the cron server (phpseclib): reaching this is remote command execution on another host, the highest-impact endpoint in the application.
CronScriptController update => [super]. Same impact as store.
ApiController store => [super]. Stores external API connection settings, credentials included.

SeedController store => [super]. NOTE: its 'index' is declared as [] — an EMPTY array, which RoleMiddleware treats as no restriction at all, so /adi/seeds is readable by any authenticated user while every other listing screen is limited to super+support. Deliberate or an oversight, it is a discrepancy worth asking the team about; it is asserted below rather than assumed.
SeedController index => [] (no restriction). Encoded as allow-both to match the code as written. If the team intends seeds to be super-only, this line is the finding, not the test.
DashboardController registers no RoleMiddleware: any authenticated user.

AnalysisController registers NO RoleMiddleware, so any authenticated user reaches the query console. Encoded as the code behaves; whether that is intended is a question for the team, and it is the single most interesting one in this matrix — /adi/analysis/query executes stored SQL.
AnalysisController has no RoleMiddleware. Executes analysis queries against newintegracion. Same question as above, with more impact.
LogController registers no RoleMiddleware: any authenticated user reads the audit log.
